title: Is it a good idea to add dynamic difficulty to games?

posts.author: oftens
posts.body:
When I was making the game, I tried to add a dynamic difficulty system to the game. As the player becomes stronger, some common monsters will become stronger, in exchange for more advantageous props.
That being said, some of my friends said that adding dynamic difficulty changes to RPG games may not be a good idea. Because many players may enjoy the joy of numerical values more, and this idea prevents them from having fun.
In many action games, dynamic difficulty is a common effect, but most of them are action games, such as The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild.
Do you think that this kind of enemy becomes stronger as the player becomes stronger, which is a challenging fun for the player, or is it a negative setting that affects the game experience?

posts.author: TRIDIUM
posts.body:
Generally, I'm not a fan.
I like being able to revisit old areas at a higher level, and for me it takes a bit away from my sense of progression if the enemies are automatically getting stronger.
Breath of the Wild is a specific case because it's open world, so enemies pretty much have to scale with the player.

posts.author: alice_gristle
posts.body:
I like to grind and to feel like it mattered, so it's a no from me as well!
Also, if ya search for a bit, you gonna notice this topic's been talked about before, sooo... revisit some of those older threads and read up on the wisdom of the ages!

posts.author: Ahuramazda
posts.body:
Personally I hate it as well, but maybe instead of forced dynamic difficulty you can add in a difficulty slider to the game and let the player control the difficult with the press of a button so to say.
If they feel its too easy just slide it up to a harder option (think torment levels on Diablo 3 as a great example), or if they have maybe set the bar too high for themselves for a new area, they can lower it back down or even make it easier than whatever "normal" may be considered.
My game does, however have a slight dynamic difficulty to it, but only for enemy attacks... enemies deal 1% more damage per player level, which doesn't sound bad considering how much more potent player stats will be in comparison, at least until they slide the difficulty on my game to max at which point enemies have 500% stats and will absolutely wreck you if you max it out too soon.
In the end it is all about testing and balancing to make sure the default experience feels good and giving the player more options to control the game themselves.

posts.author: gstv87
posts.body:
yes... but then again, no...
it's not good for anything with a story in an open world, since *because you go forward* because of the linearity of *any* story, going back to a previous area that you have cleared and finding enemies that you've outperformed and outgrown long ago suddenly *at* your current level, breaks the narrative... it makes your progress meaningless.
it is good for stories without open worlds, since you can't find an enemy from a previous instance unless it's written in the story.
you can find *that previous miniboss* now improved and up to your current challenge.
...but *it* comes to *you*, by standing in your way... not you to them by going back.

posts.author: BloodyKun

I’ve thought about it, though not in the sense of simply scaling enemies, which has already had a recent thread here I guess.
My main inspiration would be God Hand, which is pretty blatant about it, though I’ve heard Resident Evil 4 uses a similar but more hidden system as well.  I think it would be harder to find ways to implement in a turn based rpg, and I might have to be more creative and it might not even really be worth it, but I think I’d like to try and track whether a player uses this many healing items or goes through so many battles without, or how many times they flee, etc, and maybe take that all into account when loading the next area - not to punish better players but rather just to keep them from getting bored, as well as to let people who struggle have a better time learning mechanics if they need to.

Little Big Planet 2 kinda did the same, with what could be considered a hybrid approach.
at some point, aliens invade the planet, and you go to their planet to fight them off.
when you come back, your planet is taken over and there are checkpoints with armed guards.
going from one place to the other doesn't change your strength or abilities right away, but you go from zero enemies at home, to many enemies at home.
if you must change something in an open world, take the player out for a bit, and put them back.
in LBP, nothing changes until you leave, but also, the story doesn't progress *unless* you leave, so it's the same thing as a linear progression, even though the game is open (ish)
NFSU2 is another example: every round of exploration you're left to perform between story points has a number of NPC racers you can find roaming about. Every story race is scripted, but the free races scale with you, and you can't get to the next story race until you complete the required wins.
if you grind enough and unlock all the upgrades available, you're still forced to run the story race to progress, but you can keep racing as many NPCs as you want to farm coin, and they'll be at your level.... the scripted races won't be, and they won't be a challenge if you're at the level cap.

posts.author: Silenity
posts.body:
I think, like most things, it depends.
There's a difference in dynamic difficulty and scaling difficulty.
There's ways to go about it that make it more than just Player Level 1 = Enemy Level 1 and Player Level 5 = Enemy Level 5.
It doesn't have to be direct stat adjustments, but that's what most developers do, as it's the easiest and least time constraining. However, it's the form that most people don't enjoy. If I level up to deal more damage but the enemy levels up with me and increases their defense so I now deal the same damage as I was doing, that feels terrible.
When I think of dynamic difficulty, I really like that. Adapting difficulty, for example, Middle Earth Shadow of Mordor/War. The Nemesis system and how some units can adapt on the fly to your moveset if you spam the same thing too much. Like if you jump over an orc's head too much, eventually, he will start grabbing you and slamming your ass back into the ground. Preventing you from jumping over him and having to resort to a new/different tactic.
That's dynamic difficulty done right.

posts.author: Sword_of_Dusk
posts.body:
Dynamic difficulty≠enemy scaling. These are two different things, as dynamic difficulty will adjust as you play, depending on how well or poorly you're doing.
Enemy scaling is a permanent thing. Once you level, enemies do too, and there's no going back on that.

posts.author: Artille
posts.body:
In my opinion it pretty much depends on the game style you are after.
For a classic RPG style, you might not want to do that, as everyone know the G in RPG stands for Grinding.
Making the ennemies stronger based on your progress makes you lose the feeling of progress.
For a hack & slash (or abs) type of game, it might be a good idea, as you most likely don't want your players to steamroll on incoming mobs, and your players most likely want challenge as well.
So yeah, depends on the kind of game really.

posts.author: Seacliff
posts.body:
If you're scaling everything to the player's progression, it is worth considering why you have player progression to begin with.
People tend to play RPGs because they like gameplay around the growing stats, the more you overlap that with other interest the more bloat you introduce from a design perspective to take more steps to accomplish something that could have been relatively simple. You'll have an easier time designing (and a much bigger audience for your game) if you just design a game without a major progression system to begin with.

posts.author: Dunkirk
posts.body:
Is it a good idea to add dynamic difficulty to games?​
I am kind of sitting on the fence for this one, IMO it depends on what kind of games.
For MMORPG, I have seen a game implementing dynamic difficulty, by scaling down the level of players to match the level of monsters in the map, I am thinking maybe the intention of doing so, seeing that it is MMO, is to make playing together with friends more enjoyable, for example, even if you are at max level and your friend is still starting out, you will still be able to play along side your friend without your friend feeling left out and thinking, "My friend has one shot everything, I feel like I didnt contribute at all", as the max level player, you would still retain all the skills you have unlocked and be able to utilise them as combos in combat, they just do lesser damage due to your level being scaled down.
For RPG, I feel like generally most of them do not implement scaling as usually its more story driven and there is little reason to going back to older contents. Well, unless it is an idea for a challenge mode of sorts, where instead of scaling down, you scale up monsters to match the player's level, then everywhere even in beginner zones the monsters would be as tough or even tougher than the player.

posts.author: firestalker
posts.body:
So...  Umm....  my game has dynamic difficulty - kind of.
The enemies will scale with the player as they traverse the area and battle. The enemies are capped at a certain amount of growth though. They eventually stop growing and you can out-pace them. Different areas have stronger and stronger enemies, so trying to "stay weak" won't work since you have to grow to advance.
But my game has no levels only a Stat Distribution mechanic. The enemies grow with each Stat you distribute. But the Stat's grow in cost as you distribute so you have to get to the stronger enemies to keep growing since they have the higher Stat Points.

posts.author: RCXGaming
posts.body:
Let's see. Scaling is usually a bad idea, since it's easy for it to go wrong and cause an incident like FF8 where the best method of breaking the game is not to actually engage with combat but to play Triple Triad and Junction to max stats.
TRIDIUM said:
As the player, I shouldn't have to balance the game myself through a slider.
Click to expand...
Dynamic difficulty is also a tightrope to walk on, because while it's an accessibility feature for people who have different skill levels at a game, if people realize they can just game the system by turning on easy mode via slider and blow through the rest of the game then... that sort of becomes the default experience for people.
Well, people who don't arbitrarily limit themselves via challenge runs at least.
My proposed middle ground is to have Normal be the game's only difficulty, but you can pick up difficulty gems that you can switch on/off that increase enemy stats by 1.5x and boost drops + give enemies new attack patterns.
As well as areas/challenges that you can't go through them without the gems being on, so you have to endure them. To compensate, it doesn't boost enemy
defense
(since nobody likes doing scratch damage) and you the player actually get a 1.25x boost in power, effectively making it ride or die.
If a player doesn't want to do those challenges, they can leave the gems turned off.

posts.author: TG22
posts.body:
Enemy level scaling is usually a bad idea. Especially on RPG Maker.
If your enemies do not drop all the equipments that your characters could use, your players will reach a point where they are punished for leveling. Being high level with starting gear while you have to face high level enemies is not a nice experience for the player. The more you invest time in the game the more it gets difficult.
Myself, I stopped playing games early for this exact reason (Wizardry?).
Enemy Level scaling works in ARPGs because enemies have a vast pool of available loots. (For example Grim Dawn does it well, IMO). You will always get items useful for your level, the enemies' power will not grow faster than yours - if you play correctly.
In a traditional RPG/JRPG, I really prefer that you stop giving me XP if I'm overleveled. I can still continue to grind for currencies or even for fun or practicing/experimenting with the character skills you made available to me.

I really liked how Paper Mario does it where the XP tanks once you are overleveled but is never too low so you can still grind if that's what you enjoy. It does this by having you need 100 XP to level up at any level and enemies drop their "level" in XP minus your level. Once you match, they drop no XP but the end of battle "rounds" it up 1 XP.
Mind, systems aren't made in a vacuum. The on screen interaction system with enemies lets you essentially "avoid" combat when you want and the above system gives you an incentive to doing so (you're too strong, continue with the story).
